passage:
The rain had turned the railway platform into a river, and the station was packed. Baljeet stood under a leaking shed, holding his bag over his head. He had a low opinion of the police since a constable had shouted at him over a small fine the year before.
Then he heard a child crying. A girl of about four stood alone by the bench. Constable Shreya crouched in the wet, took off her own raincoat and put it on the child. "What's your name? Where were you sitting?" She spoke into the radio, called the announcement, and stayed until a woman came sprinting up the platform.
Baljeet thought of the constable who had shouted, and of Shreya. He decided he could not use one word for both.

qa.q: How old did the lost girl seem to be?
qa.a: The girl seemed to be about four.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet have a low opinion of the police at the start?
qa.a: Baljeet felt resentful and hurt because a constable had shouted at him over a small fine the year before.

qa.q: What did Baljeet decide after watching Shreya, and why is it fair?
qa.a: He decided he could not use one word for both the shouting constable and Shreya, so he judged each person on what they did instead of painting all police alike.

qa.q: What might the girl have felt when Shreya put the raincoat on her?
qa.a: The girl was probably frightened and cold while alone, and Shreya's kind questions and coat may have made her feel safer until her mother came.

grounding: A citizen sees an officer patiently help a lost child and updates a harsh view, judging fairly instead of painting everyone alike.

passage:
Jaya was on her way to work when a scooter skidded on the wet road and an elderly rider fell hard beside the divider. Traffic swelled and people stood filming. Constable Indu got there first. She stopped the cars with one hand, knelt beside the man, and said, "Stay still, uncle. Help is coming."
She called the ambulance, held his hand, and asked a bystander to bring water. When the ambulance arrived she wrote down the details and the rider's son's number.
Jaya remembered the year a police desk had brushed away her own complaint, and how sour that had made her. She watched Indu quietly and thought, some are like this too. She put her phone away and offered to help clear the road.

qa.q: What did Indu say to the elderly rider?
qa.a: Indu said, 'Stay still, uncle. Help is coming.'

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as she watched Indu?
qa.a: Jaya felt her sourness soften and some respect, as she remembered how a police desk had brushed off her complaint.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make after watching Indu, and what did it show?
qa.a: Jaya put her phone away and offered to help clear the road, and her thought that some are like this too shows she was judging individuals fairly.

qa.q: How might the elderly rider have felt while Indu knelt beside him?
qa.a: He was probably frightened and in pain after the fall, and Indu's calm voice and held hand likely made him feel safer until the ambulance came.

grounding: A citizen sees an officer patiently help an accident victim and updates a harsh view, judging fairly instead of painting everyone alike.

passage:
"Indu, you know I don't trust the police. After what happened to my cousin."
"I know, Afreen."
"But yesterday at the railway station, I saw something."
"What?"
"A little boy, maybe five, crying near platform three. Lost. People were just walking past. Then this constable came. She knelt down, gave him her water bottle, and asked his name."
"And?"
"She didn't shout for his parents. She took him to the announcement booth, made the announcement three times, and sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes."
"His family came?"
"His mother came running, crying. The constable just smiled and went back to her post."
"So... you've changed your mind?"
"Not about everything. What happened to my cousin was wrong. But I can't say they're all the same anymore."

qa.q: How long did the constable sit with the boy?
qa.a: She sat with him on the bench, holding his hand, for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she watched the constable help?
qa.a: Afreen felt surprised and moved, seeing kindness from someone she had distrusted.

qa.q: What does Afreen's changed view show about fair judgement?
qa.a: She still holds that what happened to her cousin was wrong, but she no longer paints all officers alike, which is fairer.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
qa.a: His mother was probably terrified and then overwhelmed with relief, running and crying.

grounding: A young adult who distrusts the police sees an officer patiently help a lost child and updates a harsh view, avoiding painting everyone alike.

passage:
I used to say "police are useless" at every family dinner. I'm Francis, and I had my reasons: a traffic cop once took money from my father, and I never forgot it.
Then, last winter, driving on the highway near Nashik with my friend Deepika, we saw a motorbike overturned in the fog. A man was lying on the road.
Before we could even stop, a highway patrol car arrived. The officer put out cones, covered the man with his own jacket, called the ambulance and directed traffic in the freezing cold. He talked to the injured man the whole time, calmly. He stayed until the ambulance left.
Deepika said, "That officer probably saved his life." I nodded, throat tight.
Looking back, I still remember what happened to my father. But I don't say "all police" anymore. Both kinds exist.

qa.q: What did the officer cover the man with?
qa.a: He covered the man with his own jacket.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when his throat went tight?
qa.a: Francis felt moved and humbled, seeing an officer act with care after years of believing police were useless.

qa.q: What does Francis learn about judging people fairly?
qa.a: Francis learns that both good and bad officers exist, so it is unfair to paint all police alike.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the officer's actions?
qa.a: Deepika sees them as life-saving, and seems grateful and impressed.

grounding: A young adult with a harsh view of police sees an officer patiently help an accident victim and learns not to paint everyone alike.

passage:
Senior teacher's note, Class 5 trip to the zoo, Thursday.
During the afternoon, Ujjwal, ten, wandered off near the aviary. Our new teacher, Amandeep, 24, who had told me that morning that police "never help anyone, only trouble people," was the one who noticed he was missing. She panicked.
We approached a police officer at the zoo gate. He calmly radioed his colleagues, asked for Ujjwal's description and checked the exits. Within twenty minutes, another officer found Ujjwal near the snack stall, crying, and brought him back, crouching to talk to him gently.
Amandeep thanked the officer twice. On the bus back, she said quietly, "I was so sure they were all the same. I was wrong about him."
Next step: I've suggested Amandeep lead a short class talk next week on what to do if lost, including approaching police.

qa.q: Where was Ujjwal found?
qa.a: Another officer found him near the snack stall, crying.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she noticed Ujjwal was missing?
qa.a: Amandeep felt panicked and frightened for the child.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's changed view show?
qa.a: Seeing the officers help calmly made her realise that not all police are the same, so fair judgement avoids painting everyone alike.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when the officer crouched to talk to him?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably scared and then comforted by the officer's gentle way.

grounding: A senior teacher's note records a young teacher with a harsh view of police seeing officers help a lost child, and updating her view.

passage:
Irawati's journal, Sunday.
I've always said police in this city are useless or worse. After what happened to Ayesha's brother at the checkpoint last year, I meant it.
Today, in the crowd at the old market, a little boy, maybe four, stood by the fruit stalls screaming for his mother. People stared. A constable, a heavy man with a grey moustache, pushed through, knelt right down on the wet ground and gave the boy his whistle to hold. He asked the mother's name, then got the loudspeaker shop to announce it. He bought the boy a banana. Twenty minutes later the mother came running, crying, and he just nodded and went back to his post.
I don't know what to do with that. Ayesha's brother was treated badly. This man was kind. Both happened. Maybe I have to stop saying "all of them".

qa.q: What did the constable give the boy to hold?
qa.a: He gave the boy his whistle to hold.

qa.q: What is Irawati feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Irawati feels unsettled and conflicted, holding both Ayesha's brother's bad experience and the constable's kindness.

qa.q: What fairer way of judging is Irawati moving toward?
qa.a: Judging officers one by one instead of saying "all of them", since both harsh and kind treatment really happened.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
qa.a: She came running and crying, clearly terrified and then hugely relieved to find her son safe.

grounding: It illustrates a citizen who sees an officer patiently help a lost child and updates a harsh view, recognising that both good and bad officers exist.
